claim: Biomarkers of low-grade inflammation have been associated with susceptibility to a severe infectious disease course, even when measured prior to disease onset.
source: Biomarkers of low-grade inflammation have been associated with susceptibility to a severe infectious disease course, even when measured prior to disease onset.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established finding, supported by the literature context of the study.

claim: The study investigated metabolic biomarkers measured by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy for association with susceptibility to severe pneumonia (2507 hospitalised or fatal cases) and severe COVID-19 (652 hospitalised cases) in 105,146 generally healthy individuals from UK Biobank.
source: We investigated whether metabolic biomarkers measured by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy could be associated with susceptibility to severe pneumonia (2507 hospitalised or fatal cases) and severe COVID-19 (652 hospitalised cases) in 105,146 generally healthy individuals from UK Biobank, with blood samples collected 2007–2010.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study design and sample characteristics from the abstract.

claim: Blood samples were collected from UK Biobank participants between 2007 and 2010.
source: We investigated whether metabolic biomarkers measured by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy could be associated with susceptibility to severe pneumonia (2507 hospitalised or fatal cases) and severe COVID-19 (652 hospitalised cases) in 105,146 generally healthy individuals from UK Biobank, with blood samples collected 2007–2010.
evidence: The time period of blood sample collection is explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: The overall signature of metabolic biomarker associations was similar for the risk of severe pneumonia and severe COVID-19.
source: The overall signature of metabolic biomarker associations was similar for the risk of severe pneumonia and severe COVID-19.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the Spearman correlation of 0.89 shown in Figure 7.

claim: A multi-biomarker score comprised of 25 proteins, fatty acids, amino acids, and lipids was developed.
source: A multi-biomarker score, comprised of 25 proteins, fatty acids, amino acids, and lipids, was associated equally strongly with enhanced susceptibility to severe COVID-19 (odds ratio 2.9 [95%CI 2.1–3.8] for highest vs lowest quintile) and severe pneumonia events occurring 7–11 years after blood sampling (2.6 [1.7–3.9]).
evidence: The composition of the multi-biomarker score is explicitly described in the abstract.

claim: The multi-biomarker score was associated with enhanced susceptibility to severe COVID-19 with an odds ratio of 2.9 (95%CI 2.1–3.8) for highest vs lowest quintile.
source: A multi-biomarker score, comprised of 25 proteins, fatty acids, amino acids, and lipids, was associated equally strongly with enhanced susceptibility to severe COVID-19 (odds ratio 2.9 [95%CI 2.1–3.8] for highest vs lowest quintile) and severe pneumonia events occurring 7–11 years after blood sampling (2.6 [1.7–3.9]).
evidence: The odds ratio and confidence interval are explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: The multi-biomarker score was associated with severe pneumonia events occurring 7–11 years after blood sampling with an odds ratio of 2.6 (95%CI 1.7–3.9) for highest vs lowest quintile.
source: A multi-biomarker score, comprised of 25 proteins, fatty acids, amino acids, and lipids, was associated equally strongly with enhanced susceptibility to severe COVID-19 (odds ratio 2.9 [95%CI 2.1–3.8] for highest vs lowest quintile) and severe pneumonia events occurring 7–11 years after blood sampling (2.6 [1.7–3.9]).
evidence: The odds ratio and confidence interval for long-term severe pneumonia risk are explicitly stated.

claim: The risk for severe pneumonia occurring during the first 2 years after blood sampling for people with elevated levels of the multi-biomarker score was over four times higher than for long-term risk (8.0 [4.1–15.6]).
source: However, the risk for severe pneumonia occurring during the first 2 years after blood sampling for people with elevated levels of the multi-biomarker score was over four times higher than for long-term risk (8.0 [4.1–15.6]).
evidence: The short-term risk odds ratio is explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: The prominent susceptibility to severe COVID-19 for people at high age has been linked with impaired immune response due to chronic inflammation caused by ageing processes.
source: The prominent susceptibility to severe COVID-19 for people at high age has been linked with impaired immune response due to chronic inflammation caused by ageing processes (Akbar and Gilroy, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Akbar and Gilroy, 2020.

claim: Large numbers of seemingly healthy middle-aged individuals also suffer from severe COVID-19.
source: However, large numbers of seemingly healthy middle-aged individuals also suffer from severe COVID-19 (Zhou et al., 2020; Atkins et al., 2020; Williamson et al., 2020); this could partly be due to similar molecular processes related to impaired immunity.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to Zhou et al., 2020; Atkins et al., 2020; Williamson et al., 2020.

claim: Pneumonia is a life-threatening complication of COVID-19 and the most common diagnosis in severe COVID-19 patients.
source: Pneumonia is a life-threatening complication of COVID-19 and the most common diagnosis in severe COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The main factors that increase the susceptibility for severe community-acquired pneumonia are high age and pre-existing respiratory and cardiometabolic diseases.
source: As for COVID-19, the main factors that increase the susceptibility for severe community-acquired pneumonia are high age and pre-existing respiratory and cardiometabolic diseases, which can weaken the lungs and the immune system (Almirall et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Almirall et al., 2017.

claim: Biomarkers associated with the risk for severe COVID-19 are largely shared with the biomarkers associated with the risk for severe pneumonia, including elevated markers of impaired kidney function and inflammation and lower HDL cholesterol.
source: Based on analyses of large blood sample collections of healthy individuals, biomarkers associated with the risk for severe COVID-19 are largely shared with the biomarkers associated with the risk for severe pneumonia, including elevated markers of impaired kidney function and inflammation and lower HDL cholesterol (Ho et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ho et al., 2020.

claim: Comprehensive profiling of metabolic biomarkers in prospective population studies have suggested a range of blood biomarkers for cardiovascular disease and diabetes to also be reflective of the susceptibility for severe infectious diseases.
source: Comprehensive profiling of metabolic biomarkers, also known as metabolomics, in prospective population studies have suggested a range of blood biomarkers for cardiovascular disease and diabetes to also be reflective of the susceptibility for severe infectious diseases (Ritchie et al., 2015; Deelen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ritchie et al., 2015 and Deelen et al., 2019.

claim: A broad panel of metabolic biomarkers have recently been measured using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy in over 100,000 plasma samples from the UK Biobank.
source: Conveniently, a broad panel of metabolic biomarkers have recently been measured using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy in over 100,000 plasma samples from the UK Biobank.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the available data in the introduction.

claim: Among the 105,146 UK Biobank study participants with complete data on metabolic biomarkers and severe pneumonia outcomes, and no prior history of diagnosed pneumonia, there were 2507 severe pneumonia events recorded in hospital or death registries after the baseline blood sampling.
source: Among the 105,146 UK Biobank study participants with complete data on metabolic biomarkers and severe pneumonia outcomes, and no prior history of diagnosed pneumonia, there were 2507 severe pneumonia events recorded in hospital or death registries after the baseline blood sampling (median follow-up time 8.1 years).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study results from the Results section.

claim: The median follow-up time for severe pneumonia was 8.1 years.
source: Among the 105,146 UK Biobank study participants with complete data on metabolic biomarkers and severe pneumonia outcomes, and no prior history of diagnosed pneumonia, there were 2507 severe pneumonia events recorded in hospital or death registries after the baseline blood sampling (median follow-up time 8.1 years).
evidence: The median follow-up time is explicitly stated.

claim: There were 652 PCR-confirmed positive COVID-19 cases diagnosed in hospital among the 92,725 individuals with COVID-19 data linkage available per 3rd of February 2021.
source: For the severe COVID-19 analyses, there were 652 PCR-confirmed positive cases diagnosed in hospital (inferred as severe cases in this study) among the 92,725 individuals with COVID-19 data linkage available per 3rd of February 2021.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the COVID-19 case numbers from the Results section.

claim: The median duration from blood sampling to the COVID-19 pandemic was 11.2 years (interquartile range 10.0–12.6).
source: The median duration from blood sampling to the COVID-19 pandemic was 11.2 years (interquartile range 10.0–12.6).
evidence: The time lag is explicitly stated in the Results section.

claim: There were 33 overlapping cases between severe pneumonia and COVID-19.
source: There were 33 overlapping cases between severe pneumonia and COVID-19.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Results section.

claim: Increased plasma concentrations of cholesterol measures, omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acid levels, histidine, branched-chain amino acids and albumin were associated with lower susceptibility to contracting severe pneumonia.
source: Strong associations were observed across several metabolic pathways: increased plasma concentrations of cholesterol measures, omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acid levels, histidine, branched-chain amino acids and albumin were associated with lower susceptibility to contracting severe pneumonia.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2A.

claim: Increased concentrations of monounsaturated and saturated fatty acids, as well glycoprotein acetyls (GlycA, a marker of low-grade inflammation) were associated with elevated susceptibility to contracting severe pneumonia.
source: Increased concentrations of monounsaturated and saturated fatty acids, as well glycoprotein acetyls (GlycA, a marker of low-grade inflammation) were associated with elevated susceptibility to contracting severe pneumonia.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2A.

claim: The infectious disease score comprises the weighted sum of 25 out of 37 clinically validated biomarkers, optimised for association with severe pneumonia based on one half of the study population using LASSO regression.
source: The infectious disease score comprises of the weighted sum of 25 out of 37 clinically validated biomarkers, optimised for association with severe pneumonia based on one half of the study population using LASSO regression.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2 caption and described in the Methods section.

claim: The odds for contracting severe pneumonia was increased 67% per 1-SD increment in the infectious disease score.
source: The odds for contracting severe pneumonia was increased 67% per 1-SD increment in the infectious disease score.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Results section.

claim: People in the highest quintile of the infectious disease score had close to fourfold higher risk for contracting severe pneumonia compared to those with a score in the lowest quintile.
source: This corresponds to close to fourfold higher risk for contracting severe pneumonia among people in the highest quintile of the infectious disease score, compared to those with a score in the lowest quintile.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: The association of the infectious disease score with severe pneumonia was attenuated by ~10% in magnitude when adjusting for, or omitting, individuals with a diagnosis of prevalent diseases at time of blood sampling.
source: The association was attenuated by ~10% in magnitude when adjusting for, or omitting, individuals with a diagnosis of prevalent diseases at time of blood sampling (cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, lung cancer, COPD, liver diseases, renal failure, and dementia; panels 3A and 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The association of the infectious disease score with severe pneumonia was similar across age groups, and also for men and women analysed separately.
source: The association was similar across age groups, and also for men and women analysed separately (panels 3C and 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The risk elevation for severe pneumonia events occurring 7-11 years after blood sampling was approximately half of that observed for severe pneumonia events occurring within the first 7 years (odds ratio 1.43 vs 1.75 per 1-SD).
source: The risk elevation observed in this time-lag accounting scenario was only approximately half of that observed for severe pneumonia events occurring within the first 7 years (odds ratio 1.43 vs 1.75 per 1-SD, respectively; and 2.59 vs 4.27 for individuals in the highest vs lowest quintile of the infectious disease score).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For individuals in the highest vs lowest quintile of the infectious disease score, the odds ratio for severe pneumonia was 2.59 for events occurring 7-11 years after blood sampling vs 4.27 for events within the first 7 years.
source: The risk elevation observed in this time-lag accounting scenario was only approximately half of that observed for severe pneumonia events occurring within the first 7 years (odds ratio 1.43 vs 1.75 per 1-SD, respectively; and 2.59 vs 4.27 for individuals in the highest vs lowest quintile of the infectious disease score).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The association magnitude for short-term risk (within first 2 years) of severe pneumonia was approximately twice as strong as for severe pneumonia events occurring more than 2 years after blood sampling (odds ratio 2.21 vs 1.59 per 1-SD).
source: The association magnitude in this analysis of short-term risk scenario was approximately twice as strong as for severe pneumonia events occurring more than 2 years after blood sampling (odds ratio 2.21 vs 1.59 per 1-SD; 7.95 vs 3.35 for individuals in the highest vs lowest quintile of the infectious disease score).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For individuals in the highest vs lowest quintile of the infectious disease score, the odds ratio for severe pneumonia was 7.95 for events within 2 years vs 3.35 for events after 2 years.
source: The association magnitude in this analysis of short-term risk scenario was approximately twice as strong as for severe pneumonia events occurring more than 2 years after blood sampling (odds ratio 2.21 vs 1.59 per 1-SD; 7.95 vs 3.35 for individuals in the highest vs lowest quintile of the infectious disease score).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The elevated susceptibility to severe pneumonia associated with the multi-biomarker score was three to four times stronger when examining short-term risk as compared to risk of severe pneumonia events occurring almost a decade after the blood sampling.
source: The elevated susceptibility to severe pneumonia associated with the multi-biomarker score was therefore three to four times stronger when examining short-term risk as compared to risk of severe pneumonia events occurring almost a decade after the blood sampling.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the time-dependent findings.

claim: Many of the individual biomarkers had significant associations (p-value<0.001) with increased risk for severe COVID-19.
source: Many of the individual biomarkers had significant associations (p-value<0.001) with increased risk for severe COVID-19.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Biomarkers for susceptibility to severe COVID-19 include lower levels of omega-3 omega-6 fatty acids as well as albumin, and higher levels of GlycA.
source: These biomarkers for susceptibility to severe COVID-19 include lower levels of omega-3 omega-6 fatty acids as well as albumin, and higher levels of GlycA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: There was a high concordance in the overall pattern of COVID-19 biomarker associations with severe pneumonia, with a Spearman correlation of 0.89 between the overall biomarker association signatures for severe pneumonia and severe COVID-19.
source: We observed a high concordance in the overall pattern of COVID-19 biomarker associations with severe pneumonia (Figure 2A), with a Spearman correlation of 0.89 between the overall biomarker association signatures for severe pneumonia and severe COVID-19 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7.

claim: The multi-biomarker infectious disease score was robustly associated with the future onset of severe COVID-19 with an odds ratio of 1.40 per 1-SD increment.
source: The multi-biomarker infectious disease score derived for the future onset of severe pneumonia was also robustly associated with the future onset of severe COVID-19. The odds ratio was 1.40 per 1-SD increment and 2.90 for comparing individuals in the highest quintile of the multi-biomarker infectious disease score to those in the lowest quintile.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: The multi-biomarker infectious disease score was associated with severe COVID-19 with an odds ratio of 2.90 for comparing individuals in the highest quintile to those in the lowest quintile.
source: The multi-biomarker infectious disease score derived for the future onset of severe pneumonia was also robustly associated with the future onset of severe COVID-19. The odds ratio was 1.40 per 1-SD increment and 2.90 for comparing individuals in the highest quintile of the multi-biomarker infectious disease score to those in the lowest quintile.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: The magnitude of association of the infectious disease score with severe COVID-19 was similar to that observed with severe pneumonia events occurring during the interval of 7–11 years after the blood sampling.
source: This magnitude of association with susceptibility to severe COVID-19 was similar to that observed with severe pneumonia events occurring during the interval of 7–11 years after the blood sampling.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison between COVID-19 and long-term pneumonia risk.

claim: The association of the infectious disease score with severe COVID-19 was attenuated, but remained significant when adjusted for BMI, smoking and prevalent diseases.
source: The association with severe COVID-19 was attenuated, but remained significant when adjusted for BMI, smoking and prevalent diseases (panel 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The association magnitudes of the infectious disease score with severe COVID-19 were approximately 20% weaker when limiting the COVID-19 analyses to individuals without prevalent diseases at time of blood sampling.
source: The association magnitudes were approximately 20% weaker when limiting the COVID-19 analyses to individuals without prevalent diseases at time of blood sampling (panel 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The measurement repeatability of the infectious disease score was high with a Pearson correlation of 0.94 in blind duplicate samples.
source: The measurement repeatability was high (Pearson correlation 0.94 in blind duplicate samples; Figure 9A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The levels of the infectious disease score remained broadly stable during 4 years based on blood samples from repeat visits with a Pearson correlation of 0.61 between baseline and repeat visit measurements.
source: Even though the blood samples were primarily non-fasting, the levels of the infectious disease score remained broadly stable during 4 years based on blood samples from repeat visits (Pearson correlation 0.61 between baseline and repeat visit measurements; Figure 9B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Most biomarker studies on COVID-19 have focused on characterising already infected patients and their disease prognosis.
source: Most biomarker studies on COVID–19 have focused on characterising already infected patients and their disease prognosis (Kermali et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2020; Messner et al., 2020; Dierckx et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The overall signature of biomarker associations was similar for the susceptibility to severe COVID-19 and to severe pneumonia.
source: The overall signature of biomarker associations was similar for the susceptibility to severe COVID-19 and to severe pneumonia (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by Figure 7.

claim: The proportions of individuals with existing cardiometabolic diseases were consistent for both severe pneumonia and severe COVID-19.
source: The proportions of individuals with existing cardiometabolic diseases were also consistent for both of these infectious diseases (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by Table 1.

claim: The infectious disease multi-biomarker score was largely independent of prevalent chronic respiratory and cardiometabolic diseases.
source: First, the infectious disease multi-biomarker score was largely independent of prevalent chronic respiratory and cardiometabolic diseases (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by Figure 3.

claim: The susceptibility to severe pneumonia was drastically elevated in the extreme tail of the multi-biomarker infectious disease score, with 5–10 times higher risk compared to individuals with normal levels of the multi-biomarker score.
source: Second, the susceptibility to severe pneumonia was drastically elevated in the extreme tail of the multi-biomarker infectious disease score, with 5–10 times higher risk compared to individuals with normal levels of the multi-biomarker score (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by Figure 5.

claim: The odds ratio of the multi-biomarker score for severe pneumonia events occurring after 7–11 years closely matched that of severe COVID-19, for which all events occurred over decade after blood sampling.
source: Third, the odds ratio of the multi-biomarker score for severe pneumonia events occurring after 7–11 years closely matched that of severe COVID-19, for which all events occurred over decade after blood sampling (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by Figure 4A.

claim: When confining the analyses of severe pneumonia to events occurring within the first 2 years after blood sampling, the short-term risk elevation was over four times stronger than that observed for long-term risk.
source: When confining the analyses of severe pneumonia to events occurring within the first 2 years after blood sampling, the short-term risk elevation was over four times stronger than that observed for long-term risk — individuals with high levels of the multi-biomarker score were almost 7-times more susceptible than people with low levels (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by Figure 4B.

claim: Individuals with high levels of the multi-biomarker score were almost 7-times more susceptible to severe pneumonia within 2 years than people with low levels.
source: When confining the analyses of severe pneumonia to events occurring within the first 2 years after blood sampling, the short-term risk elevation was over four times stronger than that observed for long-term risk — individuals with high levels of the multi-biomarker score were almost 7-times more susceptible than people with low levels (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by Figure 4B.

claim: Multiple blood biomarkers commonly linked with the risk for cardiovascular disease and diabetes were also associated with increased susceptibility to both severe pneumonia and severe COVID-19.
source: We observed multiple blood biomarkers commonly linked with the risk for cardiovascular disease and diabetes (Soininen et al., 2015; Würtz et al., 2017; Holmes et al., 2018; Ahola-Olli et al., 2019) to also be associated with increased susceptibility to both severe pneumonia and severe COVID-19.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The biomarkers associated with severe infections span multiple metabolic pathways, including low concentrations of lipoprotein lipids, impaired fatty acid balance, decreased amino acid levels and high chronic inflammation.
source: The biomarkers span multiple metabolic pathways, including low concentrations of lipoprotein lipids, impaired fatty acid balance, decreased amino acid levels and high chronic inflammation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: This is the first study to show that many of these blood biomarkers associate with susceptibility to severe infections.
source: This is the first study to show that many of these blood biomarkers associate with susceptibility to severe infections, potentially indicating that fatty acids and amino acids should not be considered only as biomarkers for cardiometabolic risk.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding in the Discussion.

claim: The overall pattern of biomarker associations is broadly similar to what has previously been reported with the risk for all-cause mortality in smaller prospective cohort studies.
source: This pattern of biomarker associations is broadly similar to what has previously been reported with the risk for all-cause mortality in smaller prospective cohort studies (Deelen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Deelen et al., 2019.

claim: It is unlikely that the identified biomarker signature is specific to the risk for severe pneumonia and COVID-19, or even specific to infectious diseases in general.
source: It is therefore unlikely that the identified biomarker signature is specific to the risk for severe pneumonia and COVID-19, or even specific to infectious diseases in general.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The overall metabolic biomarker perturbations observed reflect molecular signals of low-grade inflammation that exacerbate disease severity, in case of both infectious and chronic diseases.
source: We propose that the overall metabolic biomarker perturbations observed here reflect molecular signals of low-grade inflammation that exacerbate disease severity, in case of both infectious and chronic diseases (Akbar and Gilroy, 2020; Bonafè et al., 2020).
evidence: This is proposed in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Prior studies have demonstrated that elevated levels of GlycA is associated with increased neutrophil activity and the long-term risk for fatal infections.
source: In line with this, prior studies have demonstrated that elevated levels of GlycA, the biomarker with the strongest weight in the infectious disease score, is associated with increased neutrophil activity and the long-term risk for fatal infections (Ritchie et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Ritchie et al., 2015.

claim: Over-activity of immune response from pneumonia or COVID-19 infection is known to cause tissue damage and organ dysfunction through cytokine storm, a common complication of severe COVID-19.
source: Such over-activity of immune response from pneumonia or COVID-19 infection is known to cause tissue damage and organ dysfunction through cytokine storm, a common complication of severe COVID-19 (Mangalmurti and Hunter, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Mangalmurti and Hunter, 2020.

claim: The observational character of the study does not allow conclusions about whether the biomarkers are contributing causally to increase the risk or are merely indirect risk markers.
source: While the specific biological mechanisms underpinning the blood metabolic biomarker associations with chronic and infectious diseases remain poorly understood, we emphasize that the observational character of our study does not allow us to conclude whether the biomarkers are contributing causally to increase the risk or are merely indirect risk markers.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation in the Discussion.

claim: A preprint of the present study featured analysis of 195 severe COVID-19 cases, based on data available in UK Biobank back in June 2020.
source: However, a preprint of the present study featured analysis of 195 severe COVID-19 cases, based on data available in UK Biobank back in June 2020 (Julkunen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Julkunen et al., 2020.

claim: In the present updated analyses, with over three times the number of cases, all biomarker associations with susceptibility to severe COVID-19 were similar or stronger.
source: In the present updated analyses, with over three times the number of cases, all biomarker associations with susceptibility to severe COVID-19 were similar or stronger, and hereby provide a within-cohort replication of our initial findings.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as evidence of replication.

claim: A recent study used the same metabolic biomarker panel in three cohorts of hospitalised patients and observed similar overall biomarker perturbations to be predictive of COVID-19 severity.
source: In addition, a recent study used the same metabolic biomarker panel in three cohorts of hospitalised patients and observed similar overall biomarker perturbations to be predictive of COVID-19 severity (Dierckx et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Dierckx et al., 2020.

claim: The study by Dierckx et al. reported the multi-biomarker infectious disease score to be among the strongest biomarkers for discriminating COVID-19 severity among already hospitalised patients.
source: The study also reported the multi-biomarker infectious disease score to be among the strongest biomarkers for discriminating COVID-19 severity among already hospitalised patients.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion referring to Dierckx et al., 2020.

claim: The UK Biobank study participants are not fully representative of the UK population by demographic characteristics; the individuals were enrolled on a volunteer basis and are therefore more representative of healthier individuals than average.
source: Furthermore, the UK Biobank study participants are not fully representative of the UK population by demographic characteristics; the individuals were enrolled on a volunteer basis and are therefore more representative of healthier individuals than average (Sudlow et al., 2015; Fry et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The decade long duration from blood sampling to the COVID-19 pandemic limits inference on how well the biomarkers predict short-term risk for severe COVID-19.
source: Other limitations include the decade long duration from blood sampling to the COVID-19 pandemic. While this limits inference on how well the biomarkers predict short-term risk for severe COVID-19, our analogy with long-term risk for severe pneumonia indicates that the time lag likely attenuates the biomarker association magnitudes substantially.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation in the Discussion.

claim: The time lag from blood sampling to COVID-19 pandemic likely attenuates the biomarker association magnitudes substantially.
source: While this limits inference on how well the biomarkers predict short-term risk for severe COVID-19, our analogy with long-term risk for severe pneumonia indicates that the time lag likely attenuates the biomarker association magnitudes substantially.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the pneumonia analyses.

claim: Weaker biomarker associations for severe COVID-19 compared to severe pneumonia may arise from the UK Biobank COVID-19 data being influenced by ascertainment bias in terms of differential healthcare seeking and differential testing.
source: Weaker biomarker associations for severe COVID-19 compared to severe pneumonia may also arise from the UK Biobank COVID-19 data being influenced by ascertainment bias in terms of differential healthcare seeking and differential testing (Griffith et al., 2020), whereas pneumonia is anticipated to have nearly complete case ascertainment (Ho et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: A metabolic signature of perturbed blood biomarkers is associated with an increased susceptibility to both severe pneumonia and COVID-19 in blood samples collected a decade before the pandemic.
source: In conclusion, a metabolic signature of perturbed blood biomarkers is associated with an increased susceptibility to both severe pneumonia and COVID-19 in blood samples collected a decade before the pandemic.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusion of the Discussion.

claim: The multi-biomarker score captures an elevated susceptibility to severe pneumonia within few years after blood sampling that is several times stronger than the risk elevation associated with many pre-existing health conditions, such as obesity and diabetes.
source: The multi-biomarker score captures an elevated susceptibility to severe pneumonia within few years after blood sampling that is several times stronger than the risk elevation associated with many pre-existing health conditions, such as obesity and diabetes (Ho et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the conclusion with citation to Ho et al., 2020.

claim: The UK Biobank recruited 502,639 participants aged 37–70 years in 22 assessment centres across the UK.
source: Details of the design of the UK Biobank have been reported previously (Sudlow et al., 2015). Briefly, the UK Biobank recruited 502,639 participants aged 37–70 years in 22 assessment centres across the UK.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with citation to Sudlow et al., 2015.

claim: Blood samples were drawn at baseline between 2007 and 2010 in the UK Biobank.
source: Blood samples were drawn at baseline between 2007 and 2010.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: A random subset of non-fasting baseline plasma samples from 118,466 individuals were measured using high-throughput NMR spectroscopy.
source: From the entire UK Biobank population, a random subset of non-fasting baseline plasma samples (aliquot 3) from 118 466 individuals and 1298 repeat-visit samples were measured using high-throughput NMR spectroscopy (Nightingale Health Plc; biomarker quantification version 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The NMR platform provides simultaneous quantification of 249 metabolic biomarker measures in a single assay.
source: This provides simultaneous quantification of 249 metabolic biomarker measures in a single assay, including routine lipids, lipoprotein subclass profiling with lipid concentrations within 14 subclasses, fatty acid composition, and various low-molecular-weight metabolites such as amino acids, ketone bodies, and glycolysis metabolites quantified in molar concentration units.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The Nightingale NMR platform has received various regulatory approvals, including CE-mark, and 37 biomarkers in the panel have been certified for diagnostics use.
source: The Nightingale NMR platform has received various regulatory approvals, including CE-mark, and 37 biomarkers in the panel have been certified for diagnostics use.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: ICD-10 codes J12–J18 were combined to define the pneumonia endpoint.
source: We combined ICD-10 codes J12–J18 to define the pneumonia endpoint.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: 2658 individuals with recorded hospitalisation of pneumonia prior to the blood sampling were excluded.
source: Therefore, 2658 individuals with recorded hospitalisation of pneumonia prior to the blood sampling were excluded.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: 346 individuals with pneumonia diagnosis recorded in primary care settings and by self-reports were omitted from the analyses.
source: Additionally, 346 individuals with pneumonia diagnosis recorded in primary care settings and by self-reports were also omitted from the analyses.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: COVID-19 data used in the study covers test results from 16 March to 1st of February 2021.
source: We used COVID-19 data available in the UK Biobank per 3rd of February 2021, which covers test results from 16 March to 1st of February 2021.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: COVID-19 data were not available for assessment centres in Scotland and Wales, so individuals from these centres were excluded.
source: COVID-19 data were not available for assessment centres in Scotland and Wales, so individuals from these centres were excluded.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The entire study population of non-cases was used as controls in the statistical analyses (n = 102,639 for severe pneumonia and n = 92,073 for severe COVID-19).
source: The entire study population of non-cases was used as controls in the statistical analyses (n = 102,639 for severe pneumonia and n = 92,073 for severe COVID-19, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Biomarker levels outside four interquartile ranges from median were considered as outliers and excluded.
source: Biomarker levels outside four interquartile ranges from median were considered as outliers and excluded.

claim: The multi-biomarker score was trained using logistic regression with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO).
source: To minimise the collinearity of the biomarkers, the multi-biomarker score was trained using logistic regression with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), which uses L1 regularisation that adds penalty equal to the absolute value of the magnitude of the coefficients.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The multi-biomarker infectious disease score was trained using half of the study population with complete data available for the 37 clinically validated biomarkers (n = 52,573 and 1257 severe pneumonia events).
source: The multi-biomarker infectious disease score was trained using half of the study population with complete data available for the 37 clinically validated biomarkers (n = 52,573 and 1257 severe pneumonia events) using five-fold cross-validation to optimise the regularizsation parameter λ.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The number of severe COVID-19 cases in the UK Biobank closely followed the trends in hospitalised individuals for COVID-19 in England.
source: The number of severe COVID-19 cases in the UK Biobank closely followed the trends in hospitalised individuals for COVID-19 in England (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
